example.limits: Tilak's reading is one interpretation among several; it was shaped by his political context.

sources.label: Source text
sources.english: non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, calm, not slandering others, compassion for all beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty and steadiness,
sources.devanagari:

commentary.label: Commentator's view
commentary.note: Austerity and the rest purify the mind so that knowledge arises, in this life or past ones; 'and the like' includes humility and the other virtues of Gita 13.7. Truth means absence of deceit in speech, mind and body; knowledge dwells with the honest, not with the deceitful.

commentary.label: Commentator's view
commentary.note: Truth is saying what is so, without unkind falsehood; freedom from anger is calming anger that arises when one is abused or struck; not slandering is not exposing others' faults.

commentary.label: Commentator's view
commentary.note: Freedom from anger is having no change of mind that leads to harming others; compassion is being unable to bear the suffering of any being; renunciation is letting go of possessions that work against one's true good.

commentary.label: Commentator's view
commentary.note: Slander is telling a king or others of faults in order to bring trouble on someone; steadiness is not being fickle.

example.title: Death admits his own compromise
example.event: Death tells Nachiketas he knows treasure is impermanent and that the permanent is not reached by impermanent things, yet he gained his own position through ritual with impermanent means.
example.lesson: Even a great teacher can admit that their own success rests on something less than the highest; honesty about one's compromises strengthens the teaching.
example.limits: Śaṅkara reads Death's 'lasting' as only relatively lasting; the verse is not a judgement on all worldly achievement.
